\begin{abstract}
Industrial Control Systems (ICS) are evolving with advances in new technology. The addition of wireless sensors and actuators and new control techniques means that engineering practices from communication systems  
are being integrated into those used for control systems. The two are engineered in very different ways. 
Neither engineering approach is capable of accounting for the subtle interactions and interdependence that occur 
when the two are combined. This paper describes our first steps to bridge this gap, and push the boundaries of both
computer communication system and control system design. We present The Separator testbed, a Cyber-Physical testbed enabling our search for a suitable way to engineer systems that combine both computer networks and control 
systems. 
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Cyber-Physical Systems, Industrial Control Systems, Wireless Communication Networks, Testbed
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}

Industrial Control Systems (ICS) are used in civil infrastructure (water and gas distribution networks, power grids, transportation) and industrial applications
(process plants, automotive industry). 
The automation of these systems is constantly
evolving with new technologies to increase their efficiency, safety and reduce human management effort.
One area currently changing ICS is the integration of wireless communication systems. The
inclusion of new technologies creates new interactions between system components that previously did not exist. 
%\mjb{Include main argument here}
This paper presents a new ICS testbed that enables us to explore these new interactions.
%\ljb{nope, weird statement} \itc{Addresses the need could be replaced with enables to development or something that sounds more like the last sentence in the abstract. }

WirelessHART and ISA 100.11a\cite{6102417} are wireless communication protocols used for ICS 
applications. They were designed for traditional sensing applications, standardised to be 
used in industry and are used without any consideration for the influences that the
control application has on them, and the affects that they have on the control application. 
% The communication component and control component of an ICS can influence one-another. 
For instance, if network interference slows down the data rate of the sensors to the 
controller, the controller may not have the up-to-date information that it needs to maintain 
system stability. On the other hand, if the controller is using a sampling scheme that can 
vary based on system state, then a disturbance to the system may cause the sensors to
send data at a rate higher than the network channel capacity.
% Both WirelessHART and ISA 100.11a were designed to be robust communication protocols by using schemes like time division multiple access, channel hopping and blacklisting unreliable channels. 

This notion of coupling between the control system, communication system and computation is 
the core idea of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS). The aim of CPS is to develop approaches to 
engineer these coupled system components in a way that ensures the entire system meets its 
design goals of stability and safety.
%\mjb{Cyber-Physical Systems, the Systems is plural, so no need to pluralise the acronym.}

% Both WirelessHART and ISA 100.11a were designed to be robust communication protocols by using schemes like time division multiple access, channel hopping and blacklisting unreliable channels. 
% We present later in this paper evidence that WirelessHART can operate reliably in an environment with communication noise. 
% But these wireless protocols were not designed with with consideration for possible influences from other
% components of the system. 
% We advocate in this paper a way to study these influences and affects. \ljb{nope not really, same point above}

%Risk still exist for the use of wireless communication in control, despite the existence of established protocols like WirelessHART and ISA 100.11a. Wireless communication in general is always best effort, and subject to many influences. The coupling of these protocols with a control system may still cause delays and unreliablity from influences not generally considered in

%bring unreliability and latencies into the system that were previously not there when using a wired medium for communication. The current wireless communication systems have been designed to be "best-effort" and fail to provide the reliability that are needed for control system stability. \ljb{check}The interaction between the physical and the cyber worlds has led to a new research area namely CPSs. CPS is the intersection of the physical systems with the cyber world. 

A common approach to study the interactions between system components such as communication and control 
is through mathematical models and simulations. 
% This approach is difficult in this case. 
Control systems are modelled analytically using differential equations, computer systems are modelled using simulations 
and discrete mathematical representations and these models do not combine easily\cite{5995279}. There exist 
simulation environments such as Ptolemy II \cite{ptolemaeus2014system}, but they use a high level of 
abstraction and need a special notion of time to integrate the continuous and 
discrete domains. The high level of abstraction obscures realistic effects like 
radio interference, temperature effects on the physical phenomenon, etc. These effects are difficult to 
categorise and hard to include in simulation, yet they may have a large impact when these 
systems are deployed in the wild. 

%\mjb{We need to discuss how the separator fixes the high level of abstraction mentioned in the paragraph above.}
In this paper we present a CPS simulation testbed called The Separator.
It overcomes the loss of accuracy due to abstraction associated with the use of simulations 
and models. The Separator allows us to reliably emulate the behaviour of a real 
system and accurately provide the physical characteristics of sensors and actuators as well 
as the unpredictability of wireless communication systems. It also gives us the ability to 
perform repeatable experiments so that we can categorise and understand the nature of CPS 
interactions present in the system. 
%\mjb{We need to say what was missing from the other testbeds at this point.}
%A number of CPS testbeds have been proposed in 
%literature, and we discuss them later in this paper, but none of them approached control
%or wireless communication in a way that was sufficient to study the interactions inherent
%in CPS.

% We required a testbed to explore the CPS interactions in ICS. This gave us the following requirements:
% \begin{enumerate}
%     \item A non-trivial, controllable physical process.
%     \item Industrial grade sensors that communicated to the controller wirelessly.
%     \item The ability to add other sensors
%     \item The ability to use other wireless communication technologies
%     \item To be able to capture the sensor data, controller data and communication network data.
%     \item nothing about controllers, \ljb{why are there two lists?}
% \end{enumerate}
\label{specifications}
We collaborated with ABB to address the questions of the design, engineering and safety of a 
testbed suitable to explore the CPS interactions in ICS. They are keenly aware of the 
challenges, risks and issues associated with ICS engineering. Together, we developed the 
following testbed requirements.

\begin{enumerate}
    \item Have a real physical process that lends itself to control and has a well defined notion of stability and safety.
    \item Use industrial grade sensors and actuators for sensing and actuation of the physical process to  approximate the behaviour on a real ICS.  Domestic components can not handle the demands of industrial 
    applications, such as pressure for valves, current for wiring or to be operated constantly for long periods of 
    time.  %\mjb{Why is industrial important?}
    \item Control the process with an industrial grade controller that has the same performance as one that would be used on a production system. %\mjb{Why is industrial important?}
    \item Use state-of-art wireless network connecting the sensors to the controller to allow us to observe the performance of the system with different radio environments. %\mjb{Why is industrial important?}
    \item Build a system that can be used to address the issues of communication and control co-design and capture the subtle interactions between sensing, communication, control and computation. 
    \item Design a safe system that can be used by students and researchers in an academic environment.
\end{enumerate}

ABB addressed all of the diverse engineering challenges that are associated 
with the development of a CPS testbed with a real physical process. Together 
we developed \textit{The Separator, a two phase, oil and water gravity separator with senors communicating using WirelessHART that uses industrial grade components}.

In this paper we review previous approaches to the engineering of ICS systems, present the specifications of The Separator, show examples of the type of research that it is capable of,briefly describe what we have learned so far from its specification and building, and conclude with a description of the research that we intend to pursue in the future.

\section{Related Work}

% The combination of physical and computation/software components is not new. The aviation industry
% has been integrating together cutting edge technologies together years. The current safety record of the
% aviation industry clearly shows that software/physical system integration is hard to debug, and leads
% to fatalities when bugs occur. The occurrence of the same type of accident on a large scale urban or
% industrial process could affect hundreds, thousands, or more people. Therefore, a coherent design approach 
% including extensive experimentation is required to validate a system's safe and stable operation. 
%\ljb{This a really good survey, we can say a detailed review on cps methods and testbeds can be found here, we only descibr some of it, \cite{8464069}}
%\ljb{The pendulum thing is \cite{Hernandez504854}, this is the karl johansson and team}

CPS interactions can be studied with two methods. One is to use models and simulation tools and second by using tesbteds. We 
first discuss some of the CPS simulators and then describe some CPS testbeds. For a more in-depth discussion please refer to 
\cite{8464069}.

There are model based approaches that use computer systems to create models of CPSs. Systems such as
Ptolemy II \cite{ptolemaeus2014system} or GISOO \cite{6700049} combine discrete state-based models of
computer systems with continuous models of physical systems and their controllers. 
%These modelling
%platforms allow for the simulation of large-scale systems, but do not capture the subtleties and
%interactions that occur in real CPS systems 
%\mjb{Give an example of the subtleties and interactions.}
%such as the way that calibration issues with the 
%sensors can affect the ability of the controller to maintain system stability. 
%Issues such as
%the behaviour of a cold system during its
%warm-up as opposed to during its long term operation can be hard to conceive of and model. 
Modelling platforms do not use input data from real sensors and actuators that contain noise
from the physical sensing process and radio environment. This kind of noise is difficult to
correctly categorise and include in simulation, yet can have a profound impact on the system 
when it is deployed in the wild.
%In the process of abstraction, it is important to discover which details are important.

%Control of liquid levels in tanks and flows between tanks are basic problems in process industry\cite{8245161}. 

There are a number of CPS testbeds simulating smart grids and water distribution networks.
The Secure Water Treatment (SWaT) testbed\cite{mathur2016swat} was designed to assess the security 
vulnerabilities of water treatment plants. 
% In SURE tesbted\cite{Neema2016}, the authors propose an experimentation and evaluation testbed focusing on transportation networks.
The Water Distrubition Tesbted (WADI) \cite{Ahmed:2017:WWD:3055366.3055375} is used for detecting cyber-attacks and physical 
attacks. The INVITED\cite{8060334} testbed is designed to test the timing behaviours of CPSs.
In \cite{morris2011control}, the authors have created a SCADA testbed with a focus on security research. This testbed uses industrial grade sensors and controller but does not use industrial wireless protocols. In \cite{Araujo2014}, the authors use 
various aperiodic control schemes with 802.15.4 to control a double-tank system. The above testbeds have been designed for 
security research or timing analysis but none of them were designed to study CPS interactions nor do they use state-of-the-art communication protocols designed for control like WirelessHART. 
Other testbeds \cite{Hernandez504854} focus on systems with pendulums as the physical process. Although Pendulums are an 
accepted benchmark for the control theory community \cite{boubaker2012inverted}, our industrial partners suggested two-phase oil and water separation as a physical process that is more representative in the process industry.

% Another common problem with 
% CPS testbeds such as \cite{cattani2017adige}, is that they do not use industrial grade components. This 
% problem is discussed next.

%%%\mjb{Ha Ha Ha... its a Toy! Cuthbert Calculus!}
%%%\itc{Definitely remove toy...put basic or something less offending. Pendulum is the main model in the last 50 years of control theory :) 
%%%nice reference to check and appreciate more: 
%%%\url{https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233897768_The_inverted_Pendulum_A_fundamental_Benchmark_in_Control_Theory_and_Robotics}} toy

The CPS testbed that is closest to our requirements is the WaterBox\cite{Kartakis:2015:WTM:2738935.2738939}. It

\subsection{The Separator Physical Process}
Control of liquid levels in tanks and flows between tanks are basic problems in process industry\cite{8245161}. And so, the physical process that we use is oil and water gravity separation. It is used in the petroleum industry. When the petroleum mixture is extracted, the oil is mixed with water and other impurities. This mixture is put into a tank 
where the water settles to the bottom, and the oil floats on top at the rate of separation. The placement of a 
simple barrier in the middle of the tank allows one part of the tank to have only water at the bottom, and the 
other to have only oil. The water and oil can then be separated and drained into individual tanks by putting 
automatic valves at the bottom of the tank. The level of oil and water 
in the separation tank can be kept constant by controlling the degree to which the valves are open. 

The oil separation process lends itself to a clear definition of stability. The oil and the water levels, in their 
respective sections of the separation tank, are set by an operator. The controller maintains the oil and water 
levels by setting the opening degree of the valves. The degree over or under the set point of the liquid levels is 
referred to as the overshoot, or undershoot. We can use the maximum size of the overshoot above the set point as 
the measure of system stability. 

%\itc{i do not get the weak unsafety... I would go only with being unsafe when the levels are over 80\%. Amend also in II-D.}
The notion of safety is defined in terms of the stability. If the total liquid level in the tank with its overshoot are below a certain level, we can say that the system is operating safely. If the total liquid level with its overshoot exceeds 80\% of the total capacity of 
the tank, or if the water level exceeds its section and enters the oil section, we say that the system is operating in an unsafe way. 
%\mjb{How does this relate to all ICS?}
%\mjb{Why is this inherently interesting or complex}
This clean distinction between safe and unsafe states is common to all ICS applications, and gives us a clear set of parameters to use for analysis.

\subsection{The Separator Design Overview}

The design overview of The Separator is depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:separator}.

The Separator consists of two individual layers:\vspace{2pt}\\
%
\textbf{Lower layer} - A feed tank holding $100$ litres of ionised water and $105$ liters of Exxsol D-60 oil. 
The tank has two feed valves (V1 and V2), one for the water and one for the
oil. An electrical impeller pump mixes and pumps the oil and water to the upper layer.\vspace{2pt}\\
%
\textbf{Upper layer} - A $60$ litre separation tank in which the separation process occurs. The tank is
fitted with wireless sensors (P1, P2, P3 and T) and wired actuators (LV1 and LV2). The oil and water mixture is pumped 
into the separation tank by the pump mentioned above via inlet valve (V3). The separation tank
is divided into two sections by a separation plate. The left section holds water and oil and is where gravity
separation occurs. The right section receives the overflow from the left section, and contains only oil.
There are valves at the bottom of the separation tank, one in the left section which only drains water (LV1),
and one in the right section for oil (LV2). The water and oil levels are regulated by the PID controller which operates 
the valves.

% With this information it is easier to define the notions of stability and safety. We define stability as the ability of the controller to keep the overshoots of the oil and water levels within 20\% of the set point. When the system is unstable, we define the type of safety violation as the level of the overshoot. If the overshoot is above 20\%, but less than the tank capacity of $50$ litres, then the system is weakly unsafe. If the overshoot is greater than the tank capacity, then the system is strongly unsafe. The Separator is fitted with special controller settings to ensure that it never becomes strongly unsafe, this will be discussed below.

\textbf{Sensor Nodes} - The Separator has four industrial grade wireless sensors (depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:testbed}d) to measure the states of physical process. These are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Two ABB DP-Style 266DSH differential pressure sensors (P2 and P3 in Figure~\ref{fig:separator})

mixture into the tank (V3 in Figure~\ref{fig:separator}). The other two valves are controlled by the PID controller to

The controller in  Figure~\ref{fig:testbed}e is an ABB AC800M programmable automation

In the Separator we tune two basic PID controllers to control the water and oil levels in the left and right compartments. %There is a coupling between the two controllers as the oil is present in both compartments. 
The system tunes the levels of the oil first and then the levels of the water. The constant PID values are as
follows: for water $P = 1.4$, $I = 80$ and for oil $P = 2$, $I = 40$ and $D = 0$ in both cases. \vspace{2pt}\\

\textbf{Wireless Network} -
The wireless sensors communicate over WirelessHART protocol, an 
International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) approved 
wireless communication protocol for wireless sensor networks. It is based on the Highway 
Addressable Remote Transducer (HART) protocol and uses 802.15.4 in the
2.4GHz ISM band. It forms a resilient self-organising network. Sensors 
nodes can find neighbours, detect failures, form communication routes and adjust these routes
based on sensor node failure. They form a mesh topology network where each node can 
act as a router for its neighbours. Each node connects directly with a minimum of two 
neighbours in order to provide this resiliency. 

WirelessHART organises the sensors so that they can transmit their readings to a central gateway, which forwards
its data over Ethernet to the controller. The WirelessHART gateway in the Separator is the AWIN GW100 
(depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:testbed}c).

The gateway communicates using TCP
via the CI867 Modbus TCP interface to the AC800M controller.\vspace{2pt}\\

\section{Experimental Use Cases of The Separator}

In this section we present potential experimental use cases of The Separator. These include both the aspects of process 
control and system communication. We first present results showing the stability of the control process under stable 
operation. We then show how The Separator can adjust itself and maintain system stability when the oil level set point 
changes.
%to continue stable operation. 
Finally, we show the robustness of the network and the controller to local radio
interference which causes slower communication. We evaluate CPS performance with four metrics that are defined as 
follows:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textit{Latency} (in ms) - The average time required for a data packet to travel from the originating
    sensor to the controller.
    \item \textit{Path stability} (in \%) - The ratio of acknowledged packets to sent packets between two sensors or between a sensor and the gateway. 
    % Each of the two sensors keeps a separate count of the path stability denoted by $A \rightarrow B$ and $B \rightarrow A$. % A path where the two sensors have significantly different counts of path stability is called an asymmetric path.
    \item \textit{Overshoots} (OvSh in \%) - The percentage of the liquid (water or oil) above the set-point.
    This metric is important for ensuring safe behaviour of the system.
    \item \textit{Undershoots} (UnSh in \%) - The percentage of the liquid below the set-point after the first overshoot. This metric indicates the minimum level of liquid in the tank once the set-point has been reached.
\end{itemize}
The first two metrics describe the performance of the communication network, while the last two metrics describe
the performance of the control system.

\subsection{Use Case 3: Stable Operation in the Presence of Radio Interference}

The Separator contains sensors that communicate to a gateway via WirelessHART. This allows us to 
evaluate the robustness of the network and controller to adverse wireless communication conditions cause by
interference (potentially an attacker). To realise this, we used two USRP B210 software defined radios to
create white noise interference in the range of 802.15.4 channels 14, 15, 16, 23, 24, and 25. The affects are
shown in Table~\ref{tab:radiointerference}. We can see that the reliability, or percentage of messages received,
was 100\% for the entire trial. The link stability, or the number acknowledgements over the number of messages,
dropped due to the interference, and the packet delivery latency increased. The reliability of WirelessHART is unsurprising, it is a robust, multi-channel protocol that blacklists unreliable channels. Despite the robustness of WirelessHART, we can see
that the link stability and network performance were still affected by the interference. These results show that The Separator can also be used to evaluate system robustness in the presence of adverse communication conditions.

\section{Limitations and Future Research Directions}

Part of the research output of The Separator was the investigating what is needed for the research,
design, and engineering of reliable, safe CPSs. We tread the line between fidelity, with the use of industrial grade sensors, flexibility, with less robust research equipment. Things that we would consider differently would be:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Industrial grade wireless transceivers can not run different communication protocols or add more sensors. For future iterations we would search for a flexible industrial level sensor platform.
    \item The current differential pressure sensors require calibration after every run/every time the tank is drained. In an industrial setting, this calibration is not time-consuming. The processes run for a long time. In research, multiple experiments are run. Sensors that need calibration every run add an overhead, and make it difficult to obtain repeatable results. We would search for industrial grade sensors less reliant on initial calibration.
\end{enumerate}
% 1) The current industrial grade wireless sensors do not have the ability to run different communication protocols or add more sensors on the same board. For future iterations we would search for an industrial level sensor platform that could provide the level flexibility desirable in research.\\
% 2) The current differential pressure sensors require calibration after every run/every time the tank is drained. In an industrial setting, this calibration at the start of a run is not time-consuming because the processes run for a long time. In research we do experiments where we run the testbed multiple times. Sensors that need calibration every run add an overhead, and make it difficult to obtain repeatable results. For this reason, we would search for industrial grade sensors that are less reliant on initial calibration.

Finally, if we had unlimited funds we would choose to
build a larger-scale distributed system as many industrial systems are distributed over a number of
processes and over large distances. This would also allow for the deployment and evaluation of long-range communication protocols like LoRa.

A list of the future research opportunities with the current generation of The Separator, along with other associated
directions, is presented below: \vspace{2pt}\\
%
\textbf{Co-design of Communication and Control Techniques} - Explore different techniques to
co-design systems that integrate communication and control. Examine the use of \textit{formal
techniques} to model the protocol behaviour with the controller to both ensure that the
communication protocol maintains the properties required by the controller, and use \textit{run-time
verification} to check these properties during system operation.\vspace{2pt}\\
%
\textbf{Alternative Controller Schemes} - Compare of various modern
control schemes, such as \textit{event-triggered or self-triggered}, with currently used control schemes,
such as time triggered control. Experiment with other, non-conventional control approaches, such

%
\textbf{Alternative Communication Schemes} - Use wired communication protocols like HART, Profibus, Fieldbus to communicate with the sensors. Integrate different communication technologies like WiFi, 802.15.4e and bluetooth low energy into The Separator.  \vspace{2pt}\\

\section{Conclusion}

In this paper we presented The Separator, a CPS testbed whose inception and creation are part of the search
for approaches and techniques for the engineering of safe and stable CPS systems. The Separator is a result of 
the need to better understand the confluence of computer software and hardware systems, wireless communication and 
physical control processes. Preliminary experimental results demonstrate its high reliability, its use in 
performing reproducible experiments, and its ability to aid our understanding of how unreliable wireless 
communication and physical controllers can affect one another, and how to engineer this relationship to create 
stable and safe CPS.

title: Detecting Coordination on Short-Video Platforms: The Challenge of Multimodality and Complex Similarity on TikTok
summary:
Research on online coordinated behaviour has predominantly focused on
text-based social media platforms, where coordination manifests clearly through
the frequent posting of identical hyperlinks or the frequent re-sharing of the
same textual content by the same group of users. However, the rise of
short-video platforms like TikTok introduces distinct challenges, by supporting
integrated multimodality within posts and complex similarity between them. In
this paper, we propose an approach to detecting coordination that addresses
these characteristic challenges. Our methodology, based on multilayer network
analysis, is tailored to capture coordination across multiple modalities,
including video, audio, and text, and explicitly handles complex forms of
similarity inherent in video and audio content. We test this approach on
political videos posted on TikTok and extracted via the TikTok researcher API.
This application demonstrates the capacity of the approach to identify
coordination, while also critically highlighting potential pitfalls and
limitations.

\abstract{Research on online coordinated behaviour has predominantly focused on text-based social media platforms, where coordination manifests clearly through the frequent posting of identical hyperlinks or the frequent re-sharing of the same textual content by the same group of users. However, the rise of short-video platforms like TikTok introduces distinct challenges, by supporting integrated multimodality within posts and complex similarity between them. In this paper, we propose an approach to detecting coordination that addresses these characteristic challenges. Our methodology, based on multilayer network analysis, is tailored to capture coordination across multiple modalities, including video, audio, and text, and explicitly handles complex forms of similarity inherent in video and audio content. We test this approach on political videos posted on TikTok and extracted via the TikTok researcher API. This application demonstrates the capacity of the approach to identify coordination, while also critically highlighting potential pitfalls and limitations.}



\keywords{coordinated behaviour, short-video platform, TikTok, social media, multilayer network, multimodal, complex similarity}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec1}

Methods for detecting coordinated behaviour are of increasing interest in the study of online communication \citep{Manocci2024}. A key motivation is the recognition that
social media platforms, which today reach a significant portion of a population \citep{Merten2020, Reuters2024}, can serve as sites for coordinated manipulation, not least in the context of digital election interference and disinformation campaigns.
Coordination is central to problematic phenomena such as astroturfing, where several coordinated social media accounts create a false appearance of widespread and authentic grassroots support for a particular issue or cause \citep{Kovic2018, Zerback2021}. At the same time, coordination also plays a key role in earnest political campaigns and media communication strategies that lack malicious intent, yet are still worthy of study.
Existing methods for detecting coordination in social media have focused mainly on text-based platforms such as Twitter (now X) and Facebook \citep{Manocci2024, Ng2023}, but the rise in popularity of short video-based platforms poses new challenges.  
A first challenge concerns multimodality. On short-video platforms, nearly all posts integrate multiple modalities, such as video, audio, and semi-structured text, and no modality is individually sufficient to understand the post. For example, to understand a video it is typically necessary to consider both the visuals and audio.  
The second challenge is the complex similarity between posts. Assessing whether two posts enact the same message is ambiguous and technically challenging. For example, a video may be re-posted by multiple users with minor modifications, still providing a sign of potential coordination. This departs from the assumptions underpinning most literature on coordination in text-based platforms, where the posting of identical elements such as Web links is used as a signal of coordination.  
This paper presents an approach to detect coordination on short-video-based platforms that addresses these challenges. The approach has two key features. First, we address the prominence of multimedia content by accounting for coordination across multiple modalities, represented as the layers of a multilayer network. In particular, we consider music, speech, video frames, video descriptions, and hashtags, both individually and in combination. 
Second, we identify and validate functions relevant to addressing the complex similarity challenge in the short-video platform context.

We apply our approach to a prominent short-video-based platform, TikTok, which provides an archetypical representation of a recommender-based short-video system. Currently the globally most downloaded social media platform \citep{statista2024apps}, TikTok has evolved from being primarily associated with dancing and lip-syncing, to a highly relevant political environment \citep{Reuters2024}. The relevance of TikTok for the detection of coordinated behaviour was accentuated during the recent Romanian elections, where TikTok user accounts were reportedly paid to promote a pro-Russian candidate who had previously received minimal recognition and subsequently performed well in the elections \citep{tiktok_romanian_elections, ifes_romanian_election_annulment, bbc_tiktok_romanian_election}.



We work with the Researcher API to evaluate the feasibility of our approach within the constraints of the API context. Our data contains videos and slide shows posted within the two weeks prior to the 2024 European Parliament elections and is gathered using the hashtags that were used the most by German political party accounts during this period. To identify signals of possible coordination, we build a multilayer network, where in each layer two user accounts are connected based on a different type of co-action, e.g.~having posted a very similar video description at a very similar time.  
Finally, we investigate the resulting clusters of accounts, using different network filtering approaches, to identify and further examine patterns of potential coordination. 


Our approach yields evidence of potential coordination, such as accounts with similar username structure that were only active on election period. We also find different groups of user accounts in the different modalities, confirming the intuition that a multimodal approach is important in this kind of platform context in order not to miss evidence of coordination or important user groups. Some of the evidence of potential coordination is obtained thanks to the use of similarity functions matching related but not identical content, which highlights their importance in the context of video-first environments.


\section{Background}




 
This section first highlights the relevance of TikTok as a potential site of manipulated and organic political content and coordination, as evidenced by recent empirical studies. We then provide an overview of the literature on the detection of online coordinated behaviour based on the construction of networks of co-actions. 
We focus on the two main aspects that speak to the key challenges we identify with contemporary short-video centred platforms: multimodal and similarity-based coordination detection. We conclude by detailing the challenge of multimodality and complex similarity within the specifics of the features of TikTok posts and platform affordances.

\subsection{TikTok as a platform for political content dissemination}

TikTok has established itself as a politically relevant social media platform, with its own political landscape. While early influential political content was predominantly far-right \citep{Weimann2020}, the platform's user base has expanded beyond its initially primarily young demographic, broadening and reshaping the political landscape \citep{Brodovskaya2022}. Meanwhile, various types of actors are now also well-represented on the platform, including political parties, governments, news organisations, advocacy groups and political influencers.

While TikTok prohibits paid political ads, the platform has become the site for political campaigns of various kinds. Political parties across different countries use it as a platform for their campaigning 
\citep{Cervi2021, Widholm2024, Grantham2024, tiktok_politics_religion_culture, Albertazzi2023}. It is also used for protest mobilisation \citep{Brodovskaya2022, Hohner2024}, as a space for playful meme politics \citep{Vijay2021, Cervi2023, Hautea2021}, and in war propaganda \citep{Bsch2024}. 

Observers have highlighted the risk that TikTok could become a site of malicious coordinated behaviour. As noted, a key example is the risk around election campaigns, with concerns surfacing in relation to the 2024 Romanian elections \citep{bbc_tiktok_romanian_election}. One early study examined `known' coordination on Twitter and TikTok in Mexico, analysing  52 TikTok videos using content analysis \citep{Espinoza2023}. However, there has been little systematic scholarly attention to coordination and the underlying patterns or potential coordination involved in the dissemination of political messages on this platform (for a recent exception, see \cite{Luceri2025}).

Nevertheless, in principle, this is a prime area to draw on the tradition of scholarly work on the detection of coordinated behaviour that developed for other social media platforms.

\subsection{Detecting Coordinated Behaviour using Co-Actions}
\label{sec:sota_coactions}

A rich literature has emerged in the study of Coordinated Behaviour and Influence (CBI) in the context of online behaviour, including its problematic expressions. We follow Manocci et al.~in defining coordinated online behaviour as a group of users (actors), who perform synergic actions in pursuit of an intent \citep{Manocci2024}. The term ``coordinated inauthentic behaviour'' has its origin at Facebook \citep{facebook_inauthentic}, where it was used to refer to groups or accounts working together to mislead others about what they are doing. As different platforms employ different strategies and terminology, on TikTok similar actions are tracked under the term of ``covert influence operations'' \citep{tiktok_covert_influence_operations}. As noted, the work on detecting coordinated behaviour has primarily focused on Facebook and Twitter.


A powerful approach to analysing coordinated action on platforms such as Facebook and Twitter hinges on the detection of ``co-action'' in the context of a network analysis framework. In the diversity of approaches using co-actions, the majority define the term ``co-action'' as two users performing the same action on the same target or content. Therefore, co-actions can involve reacting to existing content or sharing similar posts. The most studied form is co-sharing of identical elements such as Web links \citep{Giglietto2020,Gruzd2022} and as co-retweets \citep{Nizzoli2021, Pacheco2021}, while other types of co-actions include co-commenting, co-replying, and co-liking \citep{KirdemirAA22, Jahn_2023, Manocci2024, MannocciPhD}. 

In addition to detecting the co-action itself, studies often require the co-action to occur almost simultaneously, which poses a methodological challenge in defining and identifying a cut-off point. Usually, researchers set a fixed time-frame, e.g. always one minute \citep{Soares2023} or the time-frame can be calculated based on the data such as done by \cite{Giglietto2020}. Some different approaches to deal with the temporal component in understanding coordination, are the use of a multiplex network, where the temporal component is a feature to be studied \citep{tardelli_2023}.

It would clearly be fruitful to extend the co-action framework for detecting coordination to the short-form video platforms that have become prominent in the increasingly video-first media ecology. In order to do so, however, the framework needs traction on two characteristic features of short-video platforms: their advanced multimodality and contexts of complex similarity between posts. 

\subsubsection{Multimodal coordination detection}
A handful extant studies consider multiple social media platforms together \citep{Barbero2023} or multiple co-actions (referred to as synchronised actions) \citep{Magelisnki_2021}. Only recent studies started considering multi-modality within one platform in the form of text-similarity and link-sharing \citep{DeClerck2024, Venncio2024} or different types of user actions, such as co-retweet, co-reply, or co-hashtag on Twitter \citep{MannocciPhD}. Combining multiple modalities in one approach is still a largely unexplored topic.

\subsubsection{Similarity-based coordination detection}
A small number of studies take the route of similarity-based coordination detection. Post similarity-based co-actions include co-posting, co-images, and co-videos \citep{Pacheco2021, DeClerck2024}. Within post similarity, research has mainly focused on detecting similarities in text, such as co-mentions, co-URLs, and co-hashtags \citep{Ng2023, Magelisnki_2021}. Some approaches convert images into text using machine learning to analyse descriptions rather than visuals \citep{Stampe2023}, which has been shown to better capture connotative aspects of the images \citep{Arminio25}. Studies have also explored text within images \citep{Soares2023} and metadata analysis \citep{Yu2021}. To identify similar posts, researchers create content networks (e.g.~text-text or image-image) that can be transformed into user-user coordination networks \citep{huiXian_2022, Ng2022}. 

Similar to the approach we propose in this paper, recent work on TikTok independently performed by \cite{Luceri2025} also turns to similarity functions. The study found that measures from other platforms can translate well to TikTok, such as using the hashtag-sequence, while also revealing major challenges in addressing the problem of coordinated behaviour detection on TikTok in the definition of reasonable similarity function, especially for the audio transcript.



\subsection{The challenge of multimodality and complex similarity on TikTok} \label{sec:back:tiktokdetection}

TikTok as platform creates an environment that encourages co-actions, shapes the multitude of co-action types that can occur, and at the same time poses challenges to detection in the dynamic complexity of communication that results. In addition, the specificities of the TikTok Researcher API further constrains the analytical approach that can be used. Chief among the challenges from the perspective of detecting similarities, thereby co-actions, and by extension possible coordination, are the deep multimodality of posts and the complex similarities that can be involved.


TikTok posts include a multitude of variables across several modalities that may matter for assessing similarity. Typical posts include a video description, a list of hashtags, and the actual video. When uploading a video a user is encouraged to select a music or audio snippet to layer over or instead of the original video audio. The videos themselves also comprise a number of variables, including the frames, the text displayed on the frames and the audio. This multiplicity of variables can be combined in a variety of ways in the course of the memetic communication for which TikTok is known.

A key characteristic of the TikTok environment is to encourage a memetic communication that involves the repetition, imitation and referencing of highly similar material \citep{Zulli2020, Cervi2023, Hautea2021}. Figure \ref{fig:difficulties} shows common visual alterations of videos. Often videos will have additional texts and if the original video is in a different format than the one accepted by TikTok, some users zoom in, while others autofill the space. Sometimes such visual cues are used to actually showcase disagreement with the underlying video, thus not constituting a sign of coordination.
Yet, even when the video and overall message are to all extents and purposes the same, such complex similarities in the variety of minor visual alterations makes detection much more challenging. 

Clearly, the central TikTok practice of altering videos undermines classic approaches to detecting similarity in videos posited on detecting duplicate segments. 
The largest focus for detecting video similarity is in near-duplicate video retrieval to detect copyright violation \citep{Han2021, Yang2014}. In general, reliance on duplication will not work in this environment.

Table \ref{tab:reposttiktok} sets out common ways in which TikTok users reuse existing videos, the functions by which these actions can be measured, and whether similarity can be identified by that measure. As the table makes clear, no function (or modality) is on its own sufficient to identify similar posts that may be to all extents and purposes the same.

A common user action is the traditional video repost. Being a repost, measures such as Audio (audio transcript), Music ID (the unique identifier used by TikTok for music or audio snippets), Video and Video Description remain identical. However, in the TikTok architecture, reposts do not result in a new original post; the video is added as a repost on a user's profile. As a consequence, reposts need to be searched per user account; filtering the Researcher API for videos does not return them. Another use scenario is to download and reupload a video. In this case, it appears as a new post, and the Audio stays the same, but the Music ID will be different, and additional information such as video descriptions may also be changed. 

Two further uses are presented in the possibility to duet or stitch another TikTok video, features that need to be enabled by the original poster. Duetting creates a new post, and maintains the same Audio and Music ID, but creates a split screen with the original video and audio to allow for joint dancing but also visual ``commenting". The video description may also be different. A stitch allows a commentary after the original video, therefore creating a partial audio match, meaning that the audio transcript of the initial video will be a subset of the new audio transcript. The post counts as a new post, and does not necessarily have the same Music ID, video, or description, as these features can or are automatically changed.

The overview in Table 1 highlights that no function is sufficient to identify all possible (and common) ways in which content can be the same or highly similar on TikTok. One conclusion is that a robust approach to detecting coordination on TikTok will need to be able to account for several types of multimodal combinations.

This said, another conclusion from the overview is that audio emerges as a promising key element in an approach to detect co-action in this environment. Audio stays the same across several, albeit not through all use scenarios. However, the audio transcript is not always given, but this could be countered by retrieving transcripts separately, albeit with higher computational effort. An issue to bear in mind with an approach involving any audio element is that trending audio is common on TikTok and these audio tracks can organically appear in very different contexts. This brings a risk of detecting false positives, for example videos with content referring to very different issues and contexts being linked to each other through the use of the same audio. Selecting an available audio snippet, a video will have the same Music ID as others having selected the same audio, even if different parts of the audio are selected.

\section{A Methodology to Detect Coordination on TikTok}
\label{sec:methodology}

In this work, we adopt a multilayer network-based methodology, informed by prior literature on coordinated behaviour and influence (CBI) detection (See Section~\ref{sec:sota_coactions}). Our approach is based on the concept of \emph{co-actions}, defined as instances in which users perform identical or similar actions in relation to specific content, potentially indicating coordinated behaviour.

To account for TikTok's \textbf{multimodal structure}, we construct a multilayer coordination network where each layer captures a distinct type of co-action (e.g.~identical hashtags, similar audio transcripts, matching video descriptions, shared Music IDs, or visual similarity). This multilayered actor-centric model enables us to comprehensively analyse interactions between user accounts, capturing coordination within individual modalities and across multiple modalities simultaneously.

Building this network involves first extracting and filtering relevant TikTok content (Section~\ref{subsec:data}). Each node in the resulting multilayer network represents a distinct user account, and each network layer corresponds to a specific modality-based co-action defined through tailored similarity metrics (Section~\ref{subsec:sim}). To explicitly address the second major challenge of \textbf{complex similarity}, each modality-specific layer undergoes a customized filtering process based on empirically validated thresholds (Section~\ref{subsec:filtering}). This approach ensures that minor yet significant variations --- such as slightly altered reposted videos --- are effectively captured as meaningful signals of coordination, overcoming the limitations of simpler, exact-matching methods.

Finally, the multilayer network is analysed both quantitatively, through the evaluation of structural properties like degree distributions and overlapping edges, and qualitatively, by examining the actual content within identified network clusters. This dual analytic approach allows us to reliably identify and interpret groups exhibiting potentially coordinated behaviours.


\subsection{Dataset}
\label{subsec:data}

We focus on the 2024 European Parliament election in Germany, held on June 9, 2024. Using the TikTok Research API, we began our data collection by gathering TikTok videos posted by accounts associated with the main political parties at both national and state levels, as well as their lead candidates, during the 30 day period preceding the election (i.e.~May 10 to June 9, 2024). The initial list of accounts was based on the study of the 2021 German elections by \citet{Righetti2022}. 

We then filtered the collected posts to include only those from parties that secured at least three seats in the European election, matching the minimum number of seats held by the smallest party represented in the Bundestag\footnote{The national parliament of the Federal Republic of Germany} at that time. Consequently, our filtering process excluded posts from parties with minimal media presence but retained content from most represented parties in the Bundestag, as well as some newly established parties. Notable examples include BSW and Volt. BSW is a party established only a few months prior to the EU elections, which has since gained a significant presence in the German political sphere. Volt, a smaller party, achieved notable success among younger voters during the EU campaign by leveraging social media, particularly TikTok \citep{tagesschau2024kleinparteien}.


In the second step of our data collection, we identified and selected the primary hashtag representing each party, including: \texttt{afd}, \texttt{cdu}, \texttt{bsw}, \texttt{nurmitlinks}, \texttt{freiedemokraten}, \texttt{freiewähler}, \texttt{grüne}, \texttt{spd}, and \texttt{votevolt}. Using these hashtags, we retrieved all posts containing at least one of them within the final 14 days before the election. The resulting dataset comprises 24,463 videos in various formats (e.g.~stand-alone, slideshows), including 959 videos originally posted by the main party and candidate accounts.

For each of the posts, we gathered the original TikTok video as well as the metadata associated with it. However, due to varying availability, certain metadata elements were present only for subsets of videos. Specifically, audio transcripts provided through TikTok's API were available only for 5,690 videos.
Additionally, data availability varied considerably across modalities. For instance, while TikTok's API grants access to video comments, it does not allow retrieval of comments linked to specific users. Engagement metrics face similar constraints: although likes and reposts can be obtained via user information, likes are rarely shared publicly, and collecting repost data is slow and inefficient, as the API does not support time-specific queries. These limitations informed our decision to exclude such features from the similarity functions (See Section~\ref{subsec:sim}) considered in this study.

\subsection{A multilayer approach to multimodal analysis}
\label{subsec:ml}

The next step in our methodology involved constructing the multilayer coordination network. For each modality, we compared all relevant user actions to determine whether a given pair of actions should be considered similar --- a binary decision based on the modality-specific similarity functions described below. In addition to the similarity, we annotated each pair of actions with their temporal proximity, measuring how closely in time they occurred. Once these pairwise similarities were established, we built user–user networks for each modality, where an edge between two users indicates that they performed similar actions. Edge weights reflect the number of such co-actions between the users, capturing the frequency and intensity of their potential coordination. While network analysis is a common tool to detect coordination, in this paper we use multilayer networks for the joint analysis of multiple modalities.

\subsubsection{Layer definition based on co-actions}
\label{subsec:sim}

To identify and model potentially coordinated behaviour, we constructed a set of co-action layers, each corresponding to a specific modality of similar behaviour. Each layer captures a specific type of alignment between user actions, thereby mapping user activity to interpretable patterns of content-based coordination. Some forms of similarity, like identical hashtags or video descriptions, can be captured through straightforward exact matching. Others --- particularly in the audio and visual domains --- require more nuanced computational methods to account for minor variations, edits, or transcription errors.

To validate the reliability and interpretability of these similarity metrics, we conducted a manual evaluation focused on the more complex audio and video layers. Two native German-speaking coders independently annotated 20 video pairs across 25 unique videos, evaluating similarity along three dimensions: visual similarity, audio similarity, and the underlying message conveyed. Based on their annotations, we tuned algorithmic thresholds to optimize precision and recall for the classification of both exact and partial matches. The coders reached full agreement in all but one case (95\% agreement).
 
These annotations formed the basis for establishing empirically grounded thresholds for the audio and video layers described below.

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Hashtag-Sequence.} We consider two videos part of the same co-action if they contain the exact same sequence of hashtags in their description. Videos with an empty hashtag sequence (often posted by official party accounts) are excluded. While it is common for several users to use similar hashtags to promote their videos, the use of the exact sequence might be a strong signal of resharing the same content.

    \item \textbf{Video Description.} We connect two videos if they share an identical video description. As with all layers, the resulting video-video network is projected into a user-user network layer. Exact repetition of the same description across different accounts may indicate coordinated messaging or the use of templated content.

    \item \textbf{URLs} We first extract URLs from video descriptions using regular expressions, then connect two users if they have used exactly the same URL; indicating an intent to reference the exact same content rather than the same source.

    \item \textbf{Music ID.} The Music ID is an audio identifier provided via the TikTok Research API (See Section~\ref{sec:back:tiktokdetection}). We connect two videos if they use the exact same Music ID. This identifier is assigned automatically either when a user reposts or reuses audio from another existing post --- typically by sharing or remixing that content --- or when the users manually assign a curated, trending audio during video creation. Thus, while it is possible for two users to independently select the same popular audio, it is equally plausible that shared Music IDs result from internal redistribution or imitation of existing content. This layer helps identify patterns of coordinated reuse or algorithmically encouraged convergence around specific audio trends.

    \item \textbf{Partial and same audio.} 
    Because of minor transcription errors or subtle modifications (e.g.~trimming), two videos may have identical or nearly identical audio without sharing the same audio transcript or Music ID. To capture such cases, we use edit distance metrics to measure the textual similarity of audio transcripts, quantifying how many operations are needed to transform one transcript into another. We distinguish between two types of similarity: exact audio (fully matching transcripts) and partial audio (one being a subset of the other).
    
    Using a manually labelled dataset, we identified optimal similarity thresholds based on precision-recall curves: 88 for exact audio and 68 for partial matches. Both thresholds achieved perfect precision and recall in our test set. When similarity scores spanned both categories, we selected the midpoint between the thresholds. This layer enables detection of coordinated messaging that may reuse audio content in ways not captured by TikTok's internal identifiers, such as re-recordings or minor edits.

    \item \textbf{Video Similarity.} To detect visual coordination, we apply a perceptual image hashing method that enables approximate matching between video frames. We extract one frame every three seconds and compare each frame from the shorter video to frames in the longer one, requiring that all frames have a near-equivalent match. This technique is designed to tolerate minor differences while detecting visually similar content. While the approach does not yield perfect precision and recall under a single threshold, we prioritized high precision to avoid false positives. The method performed well in identifying reused video snippets, including different cuts from the same interview, but was more sensitive to visual modifications such as zooming or autofill effects. This layer captures subtle forms of content coordination that may not be evident through audio or text alone. We apply a similarity threshold of 1, determined based on validation against manually labelled data.
\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Layer filtering and community detection}
\label{subsec:filtering}

To identify clusters of users more likely to exhibit coordinated behaviour, we applied filtering to each co-action layer by removing edges based on either (i) the \emph{frequency} of co-actions between pairs of users, or (ii) the \emph{temporal proximity} of those co-actions. The goal of this filtering process is twofold: to eliminate noisy or spurious connections and to retain structures that meaningfully reflect patterns of potential coordination.

Rather than selecting thresholds heuristically, we adopted a systematic and comparative approach. For each layer, we generated six filtered versions: three based on \emph{co-action frequency} and three based on \emph{co-action timing}.

\begin{itemize}
  \item In the frequency-based filters, we retained edges only if the number of shared co-actions between a pair of users (i.e.~edge weight) was at least 2, 10, or equal to the average edge weight for that layer. These values were chosen based on established thresholds in the literature~\citep{Soares2023, Schoch2022, Ng2023_b}.
  
  \item In the time-based filters, we retained only those edges for which the annotated time difference between co-actions was equal to or less than 60 seconds, 120 seconds, or 5 minutes. These thresholds also follow precedents in prior work~\citep{Soares2023, Ng2023_b, giglietto_tiktok_viz}.
\end{itemize}

To determine the most informative threshold for each layer, we applied the following evaluation procedure:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Edge and component pruning.} We first discarded any filtered candidate layers where too few or no edges remained, or where no connected component exceeded 8 nodes in size.

\item \textbf{Component analysis.} For the remaining candidates, we examined the structure of the largest, second-largest, and third-largest connected components. This included analysing their internal coherence in terms of shared content, behavioural similarity, and naming conventions across user accounts.

\item \textbf{Threshold selection.} We selected the optimal threshold as the one that produced the most coherent and interpretable components --- i.e.~those that clustered users together based on clear, content-driven similarities.

\item \textbf{Cross-threshold comparison.} As a supplementary check, we compared the distribution of user accounts across the different filtered networks to assess consistency and sensitivity to the chosen thresholds.
\end{enumerate}

This filtering process yielded a set of refined co-action layers, each capturing stronger and more plausible signs of coordination (See Table~\ref{tab:filtering}). Notice that the temporal proximity of interactions has not been as informative as the frequency of such interactions. We find that often similar content is posted over a longer time frame. For some of the clusters we find, some of the users in the cluster do indeed post within short time spans of each other, however filtering by a shorter time-window leads to missing the larger picture of the cluster. In addition, co-actions which are common in the data, are likely to appear within a short time-frame by chance, while the repetition of a co-action seemingly makes chance less likely. These layers formed the basis for the structural and content-based analysis presented in the following sections.

In this section, we present the results of applying our multilayer network-based methodology to the data from the European Parliament elections in the German context. Figure \ref{fig:networkvisualisation} shows the seven layers constructed from the data; structural features of the layers are indicated in Table \ref{table1}. We can find different signs of coordination across the different layers and therefore show that taking different modalities into account, is relevant for studying coordination on TikTok. Furthermore, we show that similarity measures based on audio can overcome the difficulty of recognising videos that are identical in their basis but have been slightly altered visually.

As seen in Figure \ref{fig:networkvisualisation} we find differences in network structure, edges, and user representation across the different modalities. This is partly dependent on the prevalence of the various co-actions. 
For example, when posting a video on TikTok the platform encourages the use of an existing audio (Music ID), by suggesting fitting or currently trending audio tracks, 
which leads to users to co-act more on the platform. As a result, about 50\% of the users present in our dataset, use the same Music ID as another user at least once. \subsection{Layer-by-layer analysis}

\subsubsection{Hashtag-Sequence}



The Hashtag-Sequence layer reveals clusters of potential coordinated accounts. Among the users in these clusters, we find user accounts' names starting with the word ``user" followed by a set of numbers, highlighting a potential of automated account creation. The content is usually created with little effort, as video snippets of news or talk shows are often used, while the content is commented on through text within the videos. Often this text contains a bias towards the politicians or content appearing in the videos. Most of these accounts were only active around the election time and have since stopped posting.

As an example, Figure \ref{fig:ex-hs}, shows two videos from a cluster of similar user account names. Further we find components, containing the party campaigns from the different party accounts, such as in the example in Figure \ref{fig:ex-hs:a} from the party Volt.

\subsubsection{Video Description}

This layer is related to the Hashtag-Sequence layer, because hashtags are part of the video descriptions.  
However, although all accounts in this layer also appear in the Hashtag-Sequence layer, the clustering using the video description is more distinct, with sub-clusters of accounts showing the same features. It is interesting to note that the difference in network size becomes less significant at higher thresholds for both the hashtag sequence and the video description. This suggests that for potentially coordinated clusters found through the hashtag sequence, the entire video description is often the same. Investigating the clusters, we find that users were usually only active around the election, either portraying themselves as a news platform or as a personal account. 

As an example, one component in our network consists of user accounts, where all usernames are starting with the same word (Figure~\ref{fig:ex-vd:a}). Another cluster has usernames typically starting with a female name and ending with a set of numbers (Figure~\ref{fig:ex-vd:b}). These accounts post clips from talkshows or news shows, while adding a bias through additional text in the video towards the politicians appearing in the clips. Some also include videos in ``vlogging'' style, making the account appear more authentic. However, the same person appears on multiple accounts. Most accounts were only active specifically around the European election and have since not posted.

\subsubsection{Music ID}

As we discussed in Section~\ref{sec:back:tiktokdetection}, this layer contains a lot of edges that may be the result of TikTok's recommendations more than a sign of coordination.

Nevertheless, this layer includes interesting sub-clusters that are not visible in other layers. 

As an example, we find one large cluster, where a majority of the connections are based on using the song ``L’amour Toujours'' as their audio (Figure~\ref{fig:ex-music:a}). This song has been known for its popularity within the political right wing in Germany and caught nation wide attention when a video appeared of people at a bar shouting racist sentences to the song on the 19th of May, in the lead up to the European election, causing a nation wide backlash. The cluster contains videos with the same underlying message in support of the right wing party. 
These accounts are still active today, and despite the easy-to-produce content of the post, they do not show any clear signs of automation. Therefore, this case might rather show the power of using sound as a collective, where sound creates a social bond that unites the supporters of the right-wing party. This phenomenon has been discussed in previous research \citep{Bsch2024}. 

A similar cluster, yet much smaller, is generated by the usage of audio attributed to the political left wing, such as the audio track ``N*zis raus" (Figure~\ref{fig:ex-music:b}). Interestingly, while the cluster promotes a different message, the type of content resembles the content type of the ``L'amour Toujours" cluster. Accounts post easy-to-produce content, while consisting of user accounts that remain active until now. Further, the cluster uses the ``Reclaim TikTok'' hashtag, which is a movement started in the lead up to the election.

While this is a political hashtag, it is not associated directly with one party, which might be the reason for an under-representation of the movement in our dataset.

\subsubsection{Video Similarity}


While the video similarity creates a seemingly large network, most connections are based on one video. As expected the simple measure for video similarity struggles to find many of the reposts due to the added visual changes. For example the first group in Figure \ref{fig:ex-audio:a} is not detected through the similarity measure. While the measure is not capable to detect larger clusters that showcase coordination, it does find pairs that post the exact same video, such as main party accounts reposting the video of their candidate or vice versa.

\subsection{Cross-layer analysis}

A key feature of our approach is the capacity not only to explore the different clusters and components we find in each layer, but also to combine this with looking across the layers. In principle, this should make it possible to characterise different types of coordination and coordination strategies in two regards. One is the user leveraging different modalities for strategic purposes, which could be revealed through comparing the different clusters that become apparent across the individual layers. The other concerns the multilayer signature, that is, how users engage different layers in combination. In principle, these different types may correspond to different coordination strategies in this TikTok context.

This analysis indeed reveals clusters of users that are distinct in how they leverage different modalities, indicating diverse usage trajectories and possibly different strategies. For example, Figure \ref{fig:interesting clusters} reveals clusters that can only be found on the Music ID layer (e). Given the high prevalence of Music ID in the results, it could be an attractive coordination strategy to focus on sharing music, in part to benefit from popular spread carried by the music and in part to be masked by a high amount of organic activity in the same vein.

With respect to the expectation that it might be possible to distinguish clusters that exhibit multilayer signatures, however, we were not able to identify obvious clusters of users that characteristically combine elements from multiple layers. Nevertheless, we do find multilayer signature combinations of just a few layers, especially in areas in which this would be highly expected. For example, there is a large overlap between the layers of hashtags and video description, which is where hashtags appear (a, b, d).

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
This paper presents an approach for detecting coordinated behaviour on short-video platforms that addresses the novel and challenging combination of integrated multimodality and complex similarity that is becoming prominent in a video-first environment. This approach uses multilayer network analysis as a way to identify signs of coordination within and across modalities. We focused on the case of TikTok, as a pre-eminent short-video platform, and applied our approach to communication around the European Parliament elections in the German context.


Applying our approach demonstrates its capacity to detect potential  coordinated behaviour on TikTok, but also potentially different strategies of coordination.  Like \cite{Luceri2025}, who work on US election data, we find clusters of user accounts that share similar user names. We also found user accounts that were only active during the election period. Such episodic activity is suggestive of accounts that were created for this purpose. Given the algorithmic architecture of the platform,  it is possible to get a large number of views without followers, which in turn means it is possible for custom created accounts to gain reach. 

Our proposed methodology based on multilayer network analysis shows a promising path to address coordination on short-video platforms such as TikTok. Nevertheless, there is vastly more work to be done. This includes the development and validation of additional similarity, filtering, and clustering methods for specific modalities, and further exploration of cross-layer patterns. Considering multiple layers together may reinforce the signal of coordinated behaviour,  reveal new coordination strategies, or help identifying false positives.

We note that the present application of our approach is circumscribed by the current capabilities of the TikTok Research API, such that not all meaningful similarity measures are possible to examine. For example, measures such as comments, reposts and likes are not fully accessible through the API, either because they are not made available or because it is not possible to set a time frame that would reduce the number of calls to the API to a reasonable level.  

Conversely, it is also important to consider that the areas in which organic user engagement is encouraged by the platform clouds the analysis of strategically coordinated behaviour. Our analysis shows that the similarities that the platform encourages stand out as larger networks. For example, the ease of searching content by hashtag and sound seems to find echoes in the prevalence of the same audio identifier in our results.  As a consequence our similarity detection algorithms likely detect a significant proportion of organic co-actions not based on coordination. At the same time, the popular areas also suggest styles of content that might become particularly attractive covers for strategic coordination.

We also note that while our data serves our present purposes of applying our approach, it is important to bear in mind that this paper does not report on a full empirical study of coordinated behaviour on TikTok in the German context of the European Parliament elections. This study delivers at best a partial view of communication around the elections, in part because of the character of the data set we are using. There was a time lapse between the election and the collection of the data, meaning posts may have been deleted in the interim. In addition, we focused specifically on hashtags related to the different parties, which excluded non-party actors, topics or hashtags, such as for example the ``Reclaim TikTok'' hashtag. 

A final observation concerns the importance of considered ethical reflection when working with visual content, social media data and a relatively new platform for which research best practices are not well established. To this end, we close with observing that we have, among other things, taken extra care to anonymise user account information and personal identifiers such as faces in visuals of non-public figures.

title: FinRipple: Aligning Large Language Models with Financial Market for Event Ripple Effect Awareness
summary:
Financial markets exhibit complex dynamics where localized events trigger
ripple effects across entities. Previous event studies, constrained by static
single-company analyses and simplistic assumptions, fail to capture these
ripple effects. While large language models (LLMs) offer emergent reasoning
capabilities, their direct application falters due to structural market
unawareness and limited capacity to analyze ripple effects. We propose
FinRipple, an elegant framework that empowers LLMs with the ability to analyze
ripple effects through financial theory-guided large-scale reinforcement
learning. We begin by relaxing the assumptions of previous methods,
incorporating a time-varying knowledge graph to accurately represent market
structure. By seamlessly integrating classical asset pricing theory, we align
the LLM with the market, enabling it to predict ripple effects. To the best of
our knowledge, we are the first to provide a standardized definition of ripple
effect prediction, a task that is extremely important yet unexplored in the
financial domain. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FinRipple provides a
promising solution to this task.

title: What I cannot execute, I do not understand: Training and Evaluating LLMs on Program Execution Traces
summary:
Code generation and understanding are critical capabilities for large
language models (LLMs). Thus, most LLMs are pretrained and fine-tuned on code
data. However, these datasets typically treat code as static strings and rarely
exploit the dynamic information about their execution. Building upon previous
work on trace modeling, we study Execution Tuning (E.T.), a training procedure
in which we explicitly model real-world program execution traces without
requiring manual test annotations. We train and evaluate models on different
execution trace granularities (line and instruction-level) and strategies on
the task of output prediction, obtaining around 80% accuracy on CruxEval and
MBPP, and showing the advantages of dynamic scratchpads (i.e., self-contained
intermediate computations updated by the model rather than accumulated as a
history of past computations) on long executions (up to 14k steps). Finally, we
discuss E.T.'s practical applications.

title: Topology and geometry optimization of grid-shells under self-weight loading
summary:
This manuscript presents an approach for simultaneously optimizing the
connectivity and elevation of grid-shell structures acting in pure compression
(or pure tension) under the combined effects of a prescribed external loading
and the design-dependent self-weight of the structure itself. The method
derived herein involves solving a second-order cone optimization problem,
thereby ensuring convexity and obtaining globally optimal results for a given
discretization of the design domain. Several numerical examples are presented,
illustrating characteristics of this class of optimal structures. It is found
that, as self-weight becomes more significant, both the optimal topology and
the optimal elevation profile of the structure change, highlighting the
importance of optimizing both topology and geometry simultaneously from the
earliest stages of design. It is shown that this approach can obtain solutions
with greater accuracy and several orders of magnitude more quickly than a
standard 3D layout/truss topology optimization approach.

title: Interaction, Process, Infrastructure: A Unified Architecture for Human-Agent Collaboration
summary:
As AI tools proliferate across domains, from chatbots and copilots to
emerging agents, they increasingly support professional knowledge work. Yet
despite their growing capabilities, these systems remain fragmented: they
assist with isolated tasks but lack the architectural scaffolding for
sustained, adaptive collaboration. We propose a layered framework for
human-agent systems that integrates three interdependent dimensions:
interaction, process, and infrastructure. Crucially, our architecture elevates
process to a primary focus by making it explicit, inspectable, and adaptable,
enabling humans and agents to align with evolving goals and coordinate over
time. This model clarifies limitations of current tools, unifies emerging
system design approaches, and reveals new opportunities for researchers and AI
system builders. By grounding intelligent behavior in structured collaboration,
we reimagine human-agent collaboration not as task-specific augmentation, but
as a form of coherent and aligned system for real-world work.
